{{smaller block|<poem>But herkeneth me, and stinteth now a lyte,
''Which'' a miracle ther bifel anon.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1817.}}}}

(''b'') As indicating one of a number of known or specified things: as, be careful ''which'' way you turn.
{{smaller block|<poem>Never to unfold to any one
''Which'' casket ’twas I chose.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 9. 11.}}}}

[''Which'' was formerly used as a clause-connective, along with a personal pronoun which took its place as subject or object, and rendered it redundant save as in its relative value: as, ''which . . . he'' = ''who; which . . . his'' = ''whose.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Lo! this is he,
''Which'' that myn uncle swerth ''he'' moot be dede,
But I on hym have mercy and pite.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 654.}}
<poem>The Kynges dere sone,
The goode, wyse, worthy, fresshe, and free,
''Which'' alwey for to don wel is ''his'' wone.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 318.}}
He that will mould a modern Bishop into a primitive must yeeld him to be elected by the popular voyce, undiocest, unrevenu’d, unlorded, and leave him nothing but brotherly equality, matchless temperance, frequent fasting, incessant prayer, and preaching, continual watchings, and labours in his Ministery—''which'' what a rich bootie ''it'' would be, what a plump endowment to the many-benefice-gaping mouth of a Prelate!
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}

A relic of this construction survives in the vulgar use of ''which'' as a general introductory word.
{{smaller block|“That noble young fellow,” says my general; “that noble, noble Philip Firmin.” ''Which'' noble his conduct I own it has been. {{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, xvi.}}
<poem>''Which'' I wish to remark . . .
That for ways that are dark . . .
The heathen Chinee is peculiar,
''Which'' the same I would rise to explain.</poem>
{{right|''Bret Harte'', Plain Language from Truthful James.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Which'' was formerly often followed by ''that'' or ''as'', having the effect of giving emphasis or definiteness.

This abbot ''which that'' was an holy man. {{right|''Chaucer.'']}}}}
'''The which.''' (''a''†) Who or whom.
{{smaller block|<poem>Quod she ayeyn to Mirabell here mayde,
“The same is he, ''the whiche'' I love so well.”</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2719.}}}}
(''b'') Redundant for ''which.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Lo, herte myne! as wolde the excellence
Of love agenis ''the whiche'' that no man may
Ne oght ek goodly maken resistence.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 989.}}
What is the cause of this great arising of the sands and shelves here about this haven, ''the which'' stop it up that no ships can arrive here?
{{right|''Latimer'', Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.}}}}

'''which<sup>2</sup>†''' (hwich), ''n.'' [< ME. ''whicche'', ''whyche'', ''whucche'', var. of ''hucche'', etc.: see ''hutch''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A chest. ''Halliwell.''
{{smaller block|<poem>“Rede me not,” quod Reson, “reuthe to haue,
Til lordes and ladies louen alle treuthe,
And Perneles porfyl be put in heore ''whucche''.”</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), iv. 102.}}}}
'''2.''' Specifically, a movable wagon-box.
{{smaller block|In this case the ''which'' is the movable box belonging to the tumberel, which was separated from it, and, when required, was placed upon the tumbril, to carry dung or such other materials as could not be loaded upon a mere skeleton of wheels and shafts. {{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., X. 473.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|which|6897|whiff}}</noinclude>{{nop}}(''b'') Used with reference to things, and to creatures not persons: the antecedent may also be a phrase or a clause: as, the rain washed away the track, ''which'' delayed the train.
{{smaller block|<poem>This rede pensell ye shall bere hym also,
''Whiche'' I myself enbrowdred.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3253.}}}}
{{smaller block|I declare unto you the gospel ''which'' I preached unto you, ''which'' also ye have received, and wherein ye stand.
{{right|1 Cor. xv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Next to the Guilt with ''which'' you wou’d asperse me, I scorn you most. {{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|There is one likeness without ''which'' my gallery of Custom-House portraits would be strangely incomplete.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Unto her face
She lifts her hand, ''which'' rests there, still, a space,
Then slowly falls.</poem>
{{right|''R. W. Gilder'', After the Italian.}}}}
'''2.''' As a compound relative pronoun, having the value of both antecedent and relative: as, you can determine ''which'' is better (that is, you can determine ''that'', or ''the one'', ''which'' is better).
{{smaller block|<poem>My nevew shal my bane be,
But ''which'' I noot [know not], wherefore I wol be siker.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 2660.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Are not you
''Which'' is above all joys, my constant friend?</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Even a casual reading of the statistics given above will show, it is believed, ''which'' is the more probable.
{{right|''Amer. Jour. Philol.'', X. 339.}}}}

{{smaller|''Which'' is used adjectively: (''a''†) With the sense of ‘what sort of.’}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Had thei wist witterli ''whiche'' help god hem sente,
Al hire gref in-to game gaynli schold haue turned.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2705.}}}}

'''which<sup>2</sup>†''' (hwich), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whicche'', ''whyche'', ''whucche'', var. of ''hucche'', etc.: see ''hutch''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A chest.   ''Halliwell.''
{{smaller block|<poem>“Rede me not,” quod Reson, “reuthe to haue,
Til lordes and ladies louen alle treuthe,
And Perneles porfyl be put in heore ''whucche''.”</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), iv. 102.}}}}
'''2.''' Specifically, a movable wagon-box.
{{smaller block|In this case the ''which'' is the movable box belonging to the tumberel, which was separated from it, and, when required, was placed upon the tumbril, to carry dung or such other materials as could not be loaded upon a mere skeleton of wheels and shafts. {{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., X. 473.}}}}

'''whichever''' (hwich-ev′ėr), ''pron.''   [< ''which''<sup>1</sup> + ''ever''.]   Whether one or the other; no matter which. {{smaller block|''Which-ever'' of the Notions be true, the Unity of Milton’s Action is preserved according to either of them.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 327.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whichever'' of his children might become the popular choice was to inherit the whole kingdom, under the same superiority of the head of the family. {{right|''Hallam.''}}}}

'''whichsoever''' (hwich-sọ̄-ev′ėr), ''pron.''   [< ''which''<sup>1</sup> + ''so''<sup>1</sup> + ''ever''.]   Same as ''whichever''.
{{smaller block|<poem>New torments I behold, and new tormented
Around me, ''whichsoever'' way I move,
And ''whichsoever'' way I turn, and gaze.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', tr. of Dante’s Inferno, vi. 5.}}}}

'''whick''' (hwik), ''a.'' A dialectal variant of ''quick''.

'''whickflaw''' (hwik′flâ), ''n.''   [A dial var. of *''quick-flaw'', < ''quick'', the living, sensitive flesh, as under the nails (Icel. ''kvika'', ''kvikva'', the flesh under the nails, and in animals under the hoofs), + ''flaw'', a crack, breach: see ''quick'' and ''flaw''<sup>1</sup>. Hence, by corruption, ''whitflaw'', ''whitlow'': see ''whitlow''.]   A swelling or inflammation about the nails or ends of the fingers; paronychia; whitlow. See ''whitlow''. [Prov. Eng.]

'''whid'''<sup>1</sup> (hwid), ''n.''   [Sc. also ''quhid'', ''quhyd''; cf. W. ''chwid'', a quick turn, ''chwido'', jerk. Cf. also AS. ''hwitha'', a breeze, = Icel. ''hwidha'', a puff.]   A quick motion; a rapid, noiseless movement. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>And jinkin’ hares, in amorous ''whids'',
Their loves enjoy. ''Burns'', To W. Simpson.</poem>}}

'''whid'''<sup>1</sup> (hwid), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''whidded'', ppr. ''whidding''.   [Cf. ''whid''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''1.''' To whisk; scud; move nimbly, as a hare or other small animal.
{{smaller block|Ye maukins ''whiddin'' thro’ the glade.
{{right|''Burns'', Elegy on Capt. Matthew Henderson.}}}}

{{smaller block|That creature ''whids'' about frae place to place, like a hen on a het girdle. {{right|''Saxon and Gael'', III. 104. (''Jamieson.'')}}}}
'''2.''' To fib; lie. [Scotch in both uses.]

'''whid'''<sup>2</sup> (hwid), ''n.''   [Perhaps a dial. form, ult. < AS. ''cwide'', a saying, < ''cwethan'', say: see ''quethe''.]   '''1.''' A word.   ''Harman'', Caveat for Cursetors, p. 116. [Thieves’ and Gipsies’ cant.] —'''2.''' A lie; a fib. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>A rousing ''whid'' at times to vend,
An nail’t wi’ Scripture.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Death and Dr. Hornbook.}}}}
'''3.''' A dispute; a quarrel.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] —{{smaller|'''To cut bene''' (or '''boon''') '''whids''', to speak good words.}}
{{smaller block|“Peace, I pray thee, good Wayland!” said the boy, “credit me, the swaggering vein will not pass here; you must ''cut boon whids!''” {{right|''Scott'', Kenilworth, x.}}}}

'''whid'''<sup>2</sup> (hwid), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''whidded'', ppr. ''whidding''.   [< ''whid''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'']   To lie; fib. [Scotch.]

'''whidah''' (hwid′ä), ''n.''   [Also ''whydah'', ''whidaw'', ''whydaw''; short for ''whidah-bird''; < ''Whidah'', ''Whydah'', the chief seaport of Dahomey, West Africa.]   Same as ''whidah-bird''.—{{smaller|'''Whidah thrush.''' See ''thrush''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''whidah-bird''' (hwid′ä-bėrd), ''n.''   [Also ''whydah-bird'', ''widow-bird''; < ''Whidah'', a locality in Dahomey, where the birds abound. See ''whidah'', and cf. ''Vidua''.]   An oscine passerine bird of Africa, belonging to the family ''Ploceidæ'', or weaver-birds, and subfamily ''Viduinæ'' in a strict sense, and especially to the genus ''Vidua'', or one of two or three closely related genera. {{smaller|They are small-bodied birds, about as large as a canary; but the males have several feathers of the tail enormously lengthened and variously shaped, forming a beautiful arched train. Any one of them is also called ''whidah-finch'', ''vida-finch'', ''widow-bird'', and simply ''whidah'' or ''widow'', as well as by the French name ''veuve''. The original whidah-bird, or widow of paradise, is ''Vidua'' (or ''Steganura'') ''paradisea'', described and figured under ''Viduinæ'' (which see). The king whidah-bird is ''Videstrelda regia'' (see ''Videstrelda'', with cut). The principal whidah-bird is ''Vidua principalis'' (see ''Vidua'', with cut). The South African necklaced}} whidah-bird is ''Coliuspasser'' or ''Penthetria ardens'', the male of which is 12 inches long, with a tail of 8½, and has the plumage nearly uniform black, normally varied with a scarlet (sometimes orange) necklace or collar on the foreneck. The female is quite different, and only 4¾ inches long. This bird has been known for more than a century, and has acquired an extensive and intricate synonymy, chiefly of worthless New Latin names. The other whidah here figured is also South African, and has in the male a train of several long tail-feathers resembling in development and in general effect the upper tail-coverts of the paradise-trogon; it is also very large, the male being about 19 inches long. This is ''Chera procne'', the epaulet whidah, so called from the scarlet shoulders, in translation of a French name. Its original technical name was ''Emberiza procne'' (of Boddaert, 1783, whence ''Chera procne'' of most modern writers), and it used to be called ''Emberiza'' or ''Fringilla'' or ''Vidua longicauda'', and ''Loxia'' or ''Fringilla'' or ''Chera caffra''; but it is a monotype whose {{smaller|synonymy presents no serious difficulty. It inhabits from Cape Colony to Natal and the Transvaal, and also to Benguela. Other whidah-birds are noted under ''Viduinæ'' (which see).}}

'''whidah-finch''' (hwid′ä̤-finch), ''n.'' A whidah-bird. Also ''widow-finch.''

'''whidder''' (hwid′ėr), ''v. i.''   [Cf. ''whid''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' To shake; tremble.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''2.''' To whid; whizz. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>He heard the bows that bauldly ring,
And arrows ''whidderan′'' hym near bi.</poem>
{{right|''Sang of the Outlaw Murray'' (Child’s Ballads, VI. 25).}}}}

'''whiew''', ''v. i.'' See ''whew''<sup>2</sup>, 1.

'''whiff'''<sup>1</sup> (hwif), ''n.''   [Cf. W. ''chwiff'', a whiff, puff, ''chwiffio'', puff, ''chwaff'', a gust; Dan. ''vift'', a puff, gust. Cf. also ''waff''<sup>1</sup>, ''puff'', ''fuff'', G. ''piff'', ''paff'', similar imitative words. Hence ''whiffle.'']   '''1.''' A slight blast or gust of air; especially, a puff of air conveying some smell.
{{smaller block|<poem>Pyrrhus at Priam drives; in rage strikes wide;
But with the ''whiff'' and wind of his fell sword
The unnerved father falls.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 2. 495.}}}}
{{smaller block|For when it [my nose] does get hold of a pleasant ''whiff'' or so, . . . it’s generally from somebody else’s dinner, a-coming home from the baker’s.
{{right|''Dickens'', Chimes, i.}}}}
'''2†.''' A quick inhalation of air, and especially of smoke; a drawing or drinking in of smoke; also, a draught or drink, as of wine or liquid.
{{smaller block|To entertain the most gentlemanlike use of tobacco; . . . the rare corollary and practice of the Cuban ebolition, euripus, and ''whiff.''
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whiff'', indeed, occurs in a dull, prosing account of tobacco in the Queen’s Arcadia, from which, as well as from what our author says elsewhere, it would seem to be either a swallowing of the smoke, or a retaining it in the throat for a given space of time.
{{right|''Gifford'', Note to the above passage.}}}}
{{smaller block|Then let him shew his several tricks in taking it [tobacco], as the ''whiff'', the ring, &c., for these are complements that gain gentlemen no mean respect.
{{right|''Dekker'', Gull’s Hornbook, p. 120.}}}}
{{smaller block|I will yet go drink one ''whiff'' more.
{{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, i. 6.}}}}
'''3.''' A sudden expulsion of air, smoke, or the like from the mouth; a puff.
{{smaller block|<poem>Four Pipes after Dinner he constantly smokes;
And seasons his ''Whiffs'' with impertinent Jokes.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Epigram.}}}}
{{smaller block|The skipper, he blew a ''whiff'' from his pipe.
{{right|''Longfellow'', Wreck of the Hesperus.}}}}
'''4.''' A hasty view; a glimpse; a gliff. [Prov. Eng.]—'''5.''' At Oxford and other places on the Thames, a light kind of outrigger boat. {{smaller|It is timber-built throughout, thus differing from a skiff, which is a racing-boat, usually of cedar, and covered with canvas for some distance at the bow and stern.   ''Encyc. Dict.''}}
{{smaller block|The ''whiff'' is a vessel which recommends itself to few save the ambitious freshman. . . . It combines the disadvantages of a dingey and a skiff, with the excellences of neither.
{{right|''Dickens’s Dict. Oxford'', p. 19.}}}}
'''Oral whiff''', or '''Drummond’s whiff.''' See ''oral.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
